newsitem.title: USA: Be wary of terrorists, Cohen tells U.S. troops.
newsitem.headline: Be wary of terrorists, Cohen tells U.S. troops.

text.p: Defense Secretary William Cohen on Tuesday reminded U.S. military forces to be alert for possible terrorist attack one year after a truck bomb killed 19 American Air Force troops in Saudi Arabia.

"Be wary. Be careful. Remain professional. Take care of yourselves and take care of each other," he said in a message to troops on the eve of the June 25 anniversary of a huge blast at Khobar Towers housing complex in Dhahran.

Cohen also said the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation was making progress in its investigation of the attack and that Washington remained determined "to bring the terrorists to justice." He did not elaborate.

There have been no charges filed by Saudi Arabia or the United States in the bombing and no final report has been issued on who was responsible, including whether or not the blast was supported by any outside country.

The United States, Saudi Arabia and other moderate Gulf states have meanwhile upgraded the security for U.S. forces stationed in the volatile Gulf, but Cohen stressed that force protection was a never-ending process.
"As military men and women protecting U.S. interests around the world, you face many risks," he said.

"The sobering anniversary of Khobar Towers reminds us all that force protection is everybody's mission," he said. "As you go about your duties on the anniversary of this tragic event, please take time to remember your fallen comrades and those who were wounded."
U.S. officials for months have been seeking independent verification of allegations by Saudi Arabia that Iran was behind the attack.

The FBI has several times accused Saudi Arabia of failure to cooperate fully in the Khobar Towers investigation and Cohen pressed Saudi officials for more cooperation during a visit to the Gilf last week.
A Saudi dissident who has agreed to cooperate with the U.S. investigation into the truck bombing was charged last week in Washington with conspiracy to commit murder and "international terrorism."

The indictment returned by a federal grand jury alleged that Hani al-Sayegh "was associated with a terrorist organization that actively promoted the use of violence" against U.S. citizens and property abroad in an separate, unsuccessful plot before last year's truck bombing.
The three-page indictment, released a day after Sayegh's deportation from Canada, did not identify the terrorist group. The charges carry a maximum life-in-prison sentence.
Sayegh, 28, a Shi'ite Muslim, has been identified as a member of the radical Saudi Hizbollah (Party of God).

Under a previously negotiated plea deal, Sayegh has agreed to admit his guilt to the one-count conspiracy charge, U.S. officials have said. He has agreed to cooperate in the FBI's investigation into the truck bombing at the compound that housed U.S. military personnel in eastern Saudi Arabia.
They said he may have valuable information about those responsible for the massive bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen and injured 500 others.
